newsitem.title: BRAZIL: INSTANT VIEW - Brazil's $271 mln May trade gap.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Brazil's $271 mln May trade gap.

text.p: The following are comments from economists on Brazil's $271 million May trade deficit, the best performance in the nation's trade accounts in over seven months.

JOSE CARLOS DE FARIA, economist at ING Barings: "It's not a surprise. There were strong seasonal factors improving exports, especially in coffee and soybeans, but imports are running high. May imports were a little higher than we expected.
"April and May were the peaks for exports, so from now on you should see a decline in exports and imports are likely to go up, so the trade gap will grow."

DANY RAPPAPORT, chief economist at Banco Santander in Brazil: "The trade balance is already reflecting the economic slowdown. Imports slowed some after reaching a peak in March and April. Now I see imports stabilizing, fluctuating in accordance with economic activity."

Rappaport said imports should rise in September and October ahead of the Christmas season, but added Brazil's external accounts are not worrisome in the short-term because the current account gap has been easily financed by foreign investment.
"External accounts will be a problem in the long-term if exports, especially of manufactured goods, do not improve," he said.
Economists forecast Brazil's trade deficit at between $10 billion and $12 billion this year.

ROBERTO PADOVANI, economist at Trend Analise: "May's great surprise was the imports' performance. Imports fell sharply last month and may have reflected many factors, including the impact of recent restrictions on import financing and expectations of an economic slowdown."

Padovani said it is too early to predict whether imports will keep falling in coming months. He said Brazil's trade balance is still a concern, particularly because the country has had difficulties boosting exports of manufactured goods.

"The government still has to monitor the economy in order to avoid a growing trade deficit in the second half," he added, noting that the government may eventually be forced to adopt further credit restrictions to curb consumption. ((-- James Craig and Fatima Cristina, Sao Paulo newsroom 5511 2485413))
